item.title: usb-rea generates a Linux driver for your Windows-only USB gadget
item.description: usb-rea is an MIT-licensed tool for people who own a USB gadget that only ships with a Windows program. It captures packets while you use the Windows app and generates a pyusb driver for Linux. Many years ago, I had to reverse-engineer a USB video capture card, whose vendor didn’t want to work with a company specializing in “small-volume production”. I had to capture the packets with Wireshark and manually implement code to replay URB (USB Request Block) packets using libusb, while paying close attention to timings. A tool like usb-rea would have been useful at the time. More specifically, usb-rea captures USB traffic with USBPcap or usbmon while the user clicks through the vendor app and labels the actions. The open-source program then infers the command structure (constants, counters, value fields, lookup tables, CRCs) and writes a Markdown protocol report plus a standalone Linux driver. The developer, Emir Mrkaljevic, [...] The post usb-rea generates a Linux driver for your Windows-only USB gadget appeared first on CNX Software - Embedded Systems News.

item.title: ST VL53LB is the smallest FlightSense ToF ranging sensor at just 4.0 × 1.8 × 1.0 mm
item.description: STMicroelectronics has just introduced the VL53LB (VL53LBCA), its smallest Time-of-Flight (ToF) ranging sensor, part of the FlightSense portfolio, with a size of just 4.0 × 1.8 × 1.0 mm. Like the earlier VL53L0X and VL53L1X models, it’s a single-zone ToF sensor featuring a 940 nm invisible vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser (VCSEL), but it offers a longer range of up to 8 meters and supports multi-object detection. It’s 30% smaller than the previous generation (VL53L3) and consumes just 50 µW in ULP mode, which makes it ideal for smartphones and space-constrained robotics and industrial systems. item.description: The open-source Tessera project enables neat dashboards for Home Assistant on affordable 2.8-inch to 10.1-inch ESP32 touchscreen (development) kits from CYD, Guition, and Waveshare. The Tessera firmware adds a layer to ESPHome firmware for display management, touchscreen handling, dashboard rendering, tiles, plugins, and more. It works in conjunction with the Tessera Screen Manager, which provides the Home Assistant interface to configure screens, manage layouts, install firmware, and push updates. item.description: ANAVI I2C TPM 2.0 is an open-source hardware I2C TPM 2.0 security module for Raspberry Pi single board computers based on the Infineon Optiga SLB 9673 TPM 2.0 chip. item.title: Web-based breadboard simulator lets you build circuits, fix errors, and monitor designs with a built-in oscilloscope
item.description: Dev Kapadia’s de:volt is a breadboard simulator that runs in your browser. You can place parts and wires on a breadboard, and the circuit runs live the whole time as you build it. The project aims to be as close as a real breadboard would be. It reports errors and warnings, and you can monitor pins with its built-in oscilloscope and/or multimeter. For instance, an LED with no resistor burns out, a weak battery sags under load, a motor pulls current, and a 555 on the 4-channel scope shows its timing capacitor charging and discharging. de:volt highlights: Build circuits on a virtual breadboard using the 105 parts available from the interface: resistors, capacitors, diodes, transistors, LEDs, 555 timers, 74-series and CD4000 logic, EEPROMs, motor drivers, sensors, and more. Four Arduino, BBC micro:bit, and RP2040 MCU boards are also available, and you can write and run MicroPython code from the web [...] The post Web-based breadboard simulator lets you build circuits, fix errors, and monitor designs with a built-in oscilloscope appeared first on CNX Software - Embedded Systems News.

item.title: 750 MHz GigaDevice GD32H7 Cortex-M7 MCU family gets up to 9.5MB Flash, EtherCAT for industrial applications
item.description: GigaDevice adds new industrial parts to the GD32H7 series of Cortex-M7 MCUs, running at up to 750 MHz. The new lineup includes the GD32H77R for robotic joint control, GD32H78D/77D for industrial HMI applications, GD32H78E/77E for real-time motion control, and GD32H789/779 for general industrial automation. The MCUs feature up to 9728KB of on-chip Flash, 1152KB SRAM including 640KB tightly coupled memory (TCM), and hardware accelerators for mathematical operations and digital signal processing. Depending on the variant, they also integrate a MIPI DSI display interface, an EtherCAT slave controller, industrial encoder interfaces, dual Ethernet, and three CAN-FD controllers. The devices target servo drives, humanoid robots, industrial displays, CNC machines, PLCs, and digital power systems.
